newsitem.title: USA: Senate rejects tobacco tax as part of budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Senate rejects tobacco tax as part of budget deal.

text.p: The Senate Wednesday rejected a plan to finance children's health insurance with a tobacco tax after the White House and Republicans warned it would break apart their five-year balanced budget deal.

The Senate rejected the 43 cents per pack cigarette tax 55-45 in an afternoon vote that supporters said was delayed while top administration officials called senators to make sure they would vote against it.

"It was clear that it was a deal-breaker on the budget and we want to get the budget through," said a Democratic source, who declined to be identified. The source confirmed that the White House made some calls to defeat the measure.

The defeat allowed the Senate to continue debate in an effort to hold a final vote Thursday. The House approved its version in the early hours of Wednesday after rejecting an amendment that was described as "a deal-breaker." It would have boosted funds for roads and transit by $12 billion.
Senate Budget Committee chairman Pete Domenici, Republican of New Mexico, called it a "killer amendment" and chided the president for not getting into the fight for the budget deal soon enough.

"Had it prevailed, I believe this budget agreement would have split wide open and I think amendments from all sides would have started to carry and i don't know if (we could) put it back together," he said after the vote.

The sponsors of the tobacco tax, an unlikely alliance of conservative Utah Republican Orrin Hatch and liberal Massachusetts Democrat Edward Kennedy, characterised the issue as "children versus tobacco companies."

Hatch and Kennedy said they had felt sure of victory until the calls started coming from the White House. Kennedy said he had been told by a White House staff member that Vice President Al Gore stood ready to vote with them if necessary to break a tie. Asked if this about face seemed odd to him, Kennedy replied 'yes' and declined to elaborate.
"He should have kept his hands off," Hatch said of the president after the vote.

Kennedy said the proposal would be brought up again as an amendment to other key legislation and he predicted passage the next time around. He said they lost key votes due to White House and Republican leadership arguments that its approval jeopardised the five-year balanced budget agreement.

The measure would have raised $30 billion over five years through a 43-cents a pack tax increase. Of that, $20 billion would be used to cover about 7 million children without health insurance, and the remainder would help reduce the deficit.

The budget contains $16 billion for a new programme to bring health insurance to 5 million children, about half the number thought to be uninsured and not qualified for other government aid. However, Kennedy and Hatch argued that this funding was not enough and would replace other programmes that were ending.

The budget is the blueprint for $1.5 trillion in government spending in the coming 1998 fiscal year and sets goals for deficit reduction through 2002. If the plan is adopted, this year's forecast deficit of $67 billion is expected to rise next year but start to fall in 2000 to reach a small surplus by 2002.

It does not cut government spending, but budget leaders said it would slow government growth to one percent a year from the past six percent rate. Its major savings come from $115 billion cut from Medicare for the elderly.

It also provides a net $85 billion tax cut, less than one percent of the total taxes individuals and companies will pay to the government over the five years. Raines said Republican leaders had given assurances the cut would largely benefit families with children and those in which students are seeking post-secondary education.
The agreement gave Clinton $33 billion to spend on education, the environment and other domestic priorities.
